events.excerpt: We propose an institution-managed user payment ledger for recording account debits and credits, enforcing spending capacity, and sealing account periods independently of funds settlement. Specification Draft PR #2159 Problem and scope A payment institution needs to distinguish a customer’s business entries from changes to the spending capacity it grants. It also needs to connect individual entries, current-period totals, and sealed periods when reconciling customer funds. An institution-level aggregate does not provide those per-account records. This proposal defines a common contract interface for those records and controls. It can serve an institution’s own business independently or compose with an on-chain payment protocol. It does not issue or transfer assets, establish customer identity, or prove that funds have been frozen or settled. Account model and interface Each account is scoped by (account, institution) . An institution can serve payer accounts, merchant accounts, or both; the same address at two institutions does not share records or capacity. Holding the account’s private key does not grant permission to write entries. events.excerpt: From snapshots to streams A sensor-facing agent may need to respond not just to the latest reading, but to an event that began many windows earlier, a running count, or a rule that changed while data kept arriving. That is the problem behind TimeOmni-Live, a model evaluated using LiveTS-Suite, a benchmark for Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding. The full paper describes a shift from one-shot analysis of fixed inputs toward maintaining state over an open-ended stream. The associated arXiv record identifies the same version, dated Nov. 6, 2026. Unlike a fixed-window model that receives a bounded sequence and stops, a continuous system must decide whether to respond as chunks arrive, preserve useful history, and incorporate queries or revised instructions during the stream. The benchmark tests those demands through tasks built around continuing streams and evolving instructions. What the benchmark asks LiveTS-Suite contains 5,249 streams, 15,555 annotated response events and 2.2 billion timesteps, organized into 18 tasks across six capability groups. The sequence begins with instantaneous conditions, such as recognizing a threshold, and sequential conditions that require multiple observations. It then moves to event tracking, where counts or event order matter, and event ref

Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize. events.excerpt: Benchmark contrast and calibration Researchers at Amazon recently detailed a method for optimizing Mixture of Experts (MoE) models, termed Higher-Order Pruning of Experts (HOPE). While the underlying research was detailed in an arXiv v3 paper dated Sept. 29, 2026, the team published a first-party Hugging Face article on Nov. 9, 2026, providing further context on the approach. In experiments using the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B model at a 50% pruning rate, the researchers observed a performance contrast based on the calibration data employed. The study utilized two distinct domains: Evol-CodeAlpaca-v1, which is a coding-focused calibration dataset, and SWE-Bench Verified, which serves as an agentic trajectory calibration dataset. When calibrated with Evol-CodeAlpaca, the model achieved a score of 42.33 ±1.23 on the SWE-Bench Pro benchmark. When calibrated using SWE-Bench Verified trajectories, the score was 40.78 ±0.86. For comparison, the unpruned baseline for this model was 41.82. These figures represent scores multiplied by 100, derived as means and standard deviations from three independent calibration trials. On both chains the v3 period runs from June 2023 to April 2024, when the runtimes moved to v4. Most of it belongs to ordinary accounts, not parachains. That’s 636.9 DOT across 224 accounts on the relay and 262.6 DOT across 116 accounts on Asset Hub. The account sent its whole balance, got reaped in the same transaction, and what the program had withdrawn went into the trap. events.excerpt: Goose has integrated a new mechanism for handling Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, targeting how their schemas are presented to the model. The implementation, detailed in Goose PR #13378 , adds a deferred loading strategy. This story concerns the merged Goose code change; it does not establish a separate tagged product release or a change to the MCP protocol itself. By default, Goose keeps its existing eager behavior, where tool schemas are provided to the model. Deferral is opt-in. When GOOSE_TOOL_DEFERRAL=lookup is set, Goose lists available MCP tool names in the system prompt rather than providing their schemas immediately. The model can call enable_tools with exact tool names; the selected schemas become available on the next response. The merged implementation validates those names against model-visible MCP tools. If any requested name is unknown or app-only, the enable request fails as a whole. Lookup is the only implemented strategy; the PR does not add search or wildcard matching. For builders, this creates an explicit selection step between seeing a tool’s name and seeing its schema. That can matter when designing an agent workflow: a tool not enabled is not among the schemas the model can use for its next response. But this is a change in schema availability, not a n
events.headline: Goose Implements Deferred MCP Tool Schema Loading

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, AI agents now take on paid work on-chain. The client locks the pay in an escrow, and the escrow pays the agent when the work is accepted. As this grows, each payment also has to cover others: a tax that funds public services, a fee to whoever referred the job, or the repayment of a loan the agent took to do the job. This is a draft ERC for Settlement Deductions . It lets an escrow withhold these amounts from each payout. The escrow does not need to know the rules behind them. None of them can stall the payout. It works for any task escrow, not only those used by agents. Example: a payout of 100, with a 1% tax, a 2% referral fee and a repayment of 30. The treasury gets 1, the referrer 2, the lender 30. The payee gets 67. Repository (draft text, reference policy, example escrow, tests): GitHub - unicore-gpu/settlement-deductions: ERC-8492 (draft): settlement deductions for task escrows (tax, referral fees, repayments withheld at payout, never stalling settlement) · GitHub The ERC text is ERC-draft.md in the repository. I will open the PR to ethereum/ERCs next, with this thread as its discussion link. The slot this fills Escrows for agent work end in one transfer to the payee. events.excerpt: OpenAI’s Control Room design places stop enforcement for research workloads in the inference path. The system tracks model workloads across its research infrastructure, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing and more. It also works with misalignment monitoring. Calling it a control plane is descriptive: the term captures its authorization role, not OpenAI’s official name. That distinction separates a decision to stop a job from the mechanism that prevents further output. OpenAI describes a monitor, sometimes another model inspecting a frontier reinforcement learning job, that may decide to stop it depending on the details and severity. If the monitoring system decides to stop a job, it sends that job_id to Control Room. Control Room records that the job is terminated. On the next inference request carrying that ID, the service denies the request and the engine refuses further output. The monitor may make the stop decision; the inference path enforces it. When a job starts, workload code requests a job_id. Subsequent inference requests pass the ID to the engine, which asks Control Room for authorization before fulfilling them. OpenAI requires every research workload doing agentic inference to have an approved safety case. A workload may use s
events.headline: OpenAI Moves Research Stop Enforcement Into the Inference Path

events.excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. events.headline: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

events.excerpt: Elysium is live on mainnet. Developed by Kinetiq , it is the first dedicated blockchain built with the Arbitrum Platform to settle on HyperEVM, Hyperliquid’s smart contract environment, and uses HYPE as its native gas token. More capacity for established markets Kinetiq will combine Hyperliquid’s established trading markets with execution capacity tailored to high-frequency trading systems and market-making AMMs. Those markets already serve significant demand: as of November 9, 2026, Hyperliquid’s perpetual markets had processed more than $239 billion in notional trading volume over the preceding 30 days, with approximately $7 billion in open interest , according to DefiLlama . Using the Arbitrum Platform enabled Kinetiq to configure Elysium for applications that need to update prices, manage inventory, and respond quickly as markets move. Planned post-launch HyperCore integrations would let those applications use market data and send trading instructions through authorized, trade-only agents. Application logic would run on Elysium, with trades executing separately on HyperCore’s orderbooks. Introduction The program aimed to make professional security audits more accessible to teams building on Arbitrum. With its first year of applications now concluded, this report reviews the principal results and lessons emerging from its delivery. Over the year, the program progressed from establishing its evaluation and auditor-matching processes in the first quarter to managing a sustained pipeline of applications thereafter. Application volumes increased in the second half of the program, with Q4 recording the highest quarterly intake. Across the Arbitrum Audit Program, 367 applications were submitted in total . events.excerpt: This is the discussion thread for EIP-8487 (PR: Add EIP: Separate execution credits and billing credits by Giulio2002 · Pull Request #12637 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub ). The proposal introduces two counters, both initialized from tx.gasLimit : Credits follow the legacy gas schedule and are the only gas the EVM sees (GAS opcode, call forwarding, creation). Billing follows the new schedule and determines the transaction fee. If billing runs out, the whole transaction aborts (uncatchable), even if credits remain. The goal is to let opcodes be repriced without changing execution behavior for contracts that inspect or forward gas. Open questions: the exact schedules, charge points, rebate rules, receipt fields and block accounting. Feedback welcome. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full topic
events.headline: EIP-8487: Separate execution credits and billing credits

events.excerpt: Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components. The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, Texas, alongside the rise of agentic robotics — a new paradigm that integrates frontier agents to create interpretable code for physical robotics systems. At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing new open robotics technologies, including world action models , simulation tools, benchmarks and agentic workflows. Two NVIDIA papers are among six finalists out of thousands of submissions for the Best Paper Awards at CoRL: GRAIL (Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models), which presents a digital generation pipeline for 3D assets and simulator-ready scenes for robot learning. RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies , which introduces a robot model and training recipe that scales visuomotor context three orders of magnitude beyond state-of-the-art policies without growing inference latency. These advancements help researchers train robots on complex tasks, evaluate their performance across changing conditions and use failu

events.excerpt: Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem. When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start. Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent. AI is changing open source AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests. The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown. During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase. AI has raised the pressure to produce . events.excerpt: This release removes Bitswap in favour of shrex, adds JWT token revocation, and ships a set of security and stability fixes. It is compatible with celestia-app v10 and with v0.34.x nodes on the network, so no coordinated upgrade is needed. It is recommended to upgrade. Action Recommended: run config-update This release removes the unused Share.UseShareExchange , Share.UseBitswap and Share.BlockStoreCacheSize keys from the config. Nodes start without this step and ignore the old keys. To remove them from your config.toml , stop the node, upgrade the binary and, before starting the node , run: celestia bridge config-update --p2p.network corto celestia light config-update --p2p.network corto Your custom values for the other fields are kept. Review your config.toml afterwards to confirm. Breaking changes & upgrade notes Bitswap removed: shrex is now the only share exchange protocol ( #5378 ). v0.35.0 nodes keep working with v0.34.x peers, which already used shrex first and Bitswap only as a fallback. The Share.UseShareExchange , Share.UseBitswap and Share.BlockStoreCacheSize config options are removed. Existing config files still load and the keys are ignored.
